fixes.explanation: Solomon, David's son (2 Samuel 12:24), is a good guess, since the name sits right next to David's. But the verse names David's days for this count. Same family, one name over. Close, friend, and no crumbs lost.

Not quite, friend. The verse gives a reason for the 36,000 troops, and it isn't hired soldiers. It says they had that many troops "…for they had many wives and children." The reason is right there in their own household. That's a lot of family dinners.

Right, friend. The text gives the reason in plain words: "…for they had many wives and children." Hired soldiers from other lands aren't the reason it names. The 36,000 troops are tied to that big household. That's a family reunion with a draft number.

That's right. The text says, "Their father Ephraim mourned for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him." Ezer and Elead were killed, and their father grieved them. I like that his relatives came to him. I think that's what comfort looks like.

Caleb, a man from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6), is a famous name from Joshua's day, so I see why he came to mind. But this verse says Nun's son is Joshua. Caleb isn't in this part of the list. Right neighborhood, friend, different house.
That's right. Beriah and Shema were heads of families living in Aijalon. The same verse says they drove out the inhabitants of Gath. Two things in one sentence. That's a busy verse.

Yes, Gath is the second blank. The verse says Beriah and Shema "…drove out the inhabitants of Gath…" Earlier in the passage, the natives of Gath are the ones who killed Ephraim's sons (1 Chronicles 7:21). I'll just let you notice that yourself.

Moab does show up in this chapter, because Shaharaim had sons there (1 Chronicles 8:8). But that's a different man in a different verse. For Beriah and Shema, the verse names Aijalon and Gath. Moab is the right chapter, friend, just another family.
Hebron is a real city with real history. David ruled from there for a time (2 Samuel 2:11). But this verse says these chiefs lived in Jerusalem. Good guess, friend, different city.
David was Jesse's son (1 Samuel 17:12), so he's in a different family line altogether. In this verse, Kish's son is Saul. Easy to swap them, friend, since their names come up together so often.

That's right. The verse says Ulam's sons were "…mighty men of valor, archers…" The verse also says they had 150 sons and grandsons in all. That's a lot of family in one verse. I'd stay out of Ulam's backyard.
